strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck: inference latency of high-resolution diffusion transformers. A training-free spatial acceleration method that is complementary to temporal caching would be practically useful if released with reliable implementation details.

The core idea is clear and reasonably well motivated: low-resolution denoising for global structure, early high-resolution treatment of edge-prone regions to reduce aliasing, then full-resolution refinement. The paper identifies two artifact sources, aliasing and noise/timestep mismatch, and proposes targeted mechanisms for each.

The method is evaluated on two strong flow-matching T2I backbones, FLUX.1-dev and SD3, with multiple acceleration regimes. Reported speedups are meaningful: about 4.1x and 7.0x for FLUX, and about 1.9x and 3.0x for SD3, with latency and TFLOP reporting rather than only theoretical claims.

The quantitative results are encouraging. RALU usually improves over Bottleneck Sampling and temporal baselines on image-quality metrics while maintaining competitive or better text-alignment metrics. The additional caching experiment supports the claim that the method can combine with temporal acceleration.

The manuscript includes ablations for NT-DM and upsampling ratio, qualitative comparisons, uncurated FLUX samples, and a limitation section. These help substantiate the practical behavior beyond a single headline table.
weaknesses: Some important implementation details are underspecified for reproducibility. In particular, the exact mixed-resolution token representation in Stage 2, how selected high-resolution patches interact with remaining low-resolution regions inside the DiT, positional encoding handling, boundary treatment between resolutions, and the default top-k or upsampling ratio used in the main tables are not fully clear from the manuscript.

The ablation evidence is limited relative to the method’s moving parts. NT-DM is evaluated only by small perturbations of the chosen parameters and on a narrow set of metrics; the paper would be stronger with direct ablations of edge-based selection versus random/saliency/attention selection, varying Stage 1/2/3 allocations, and isolating correlated noise from timestep rescheduling across both FLUX and SD3.

The evaluation relies heavily on automatic metrics whose interpretation is not always straightforward for generative image quality. Several accelerated settings obtain better FID than the unaccelerated base model, which may be possible but raises questions about the FID dataset/protocol and whether the metric reflects perceptual fidelity. No human preference study or artifact-specific metric is provided despite the paper’s focus on visual artifacts.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. ToCa performs extremely poorly in some FLUX settings and reaches only about 5x speedup in the nominal 7x comparison, while RAS is only used for SD3. The paper gives parameter settings, but it is not clear whether baselines were tuned comparably for the same quality-latency frontier or whether stronger current acceleration combinations are omitted.

The scope is narrower than some claims suggest. NT-DM is tailored to flow-matching models, experiments are limited to text-to-image generation with two backbones, and the method’s behavior on other diffusion parameterizations, video, editing/control tasks, non-1024 resolutions, and prompts with small/thin structures is not established.

Presentation has several rough edges that affect clarity: some equations and figure references appear malformed, there are grammar issues, and one reference appears mismatched for SD3. These are not fatal, but they make the technical argument harder to audit.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: inference acceleration for large diffusion transformers, especially FLUX and SD3, where spatial token count is a real bottleneck.

The proposed three-stage framework is conceptually reasonable: low-resolution denoising, early upsampling of edge-heavy regions, and final full-resolution refinement. The motivation around aliasing near boundaries is intuitive and supported by qualitative examples.

The method is training-free and reports actual latency and FLOPs, not only theoretical complexity. Evaluation covers two strong DiT text-to-image models and several metrics for image quality and text alignment.
The idea appears complementary to temporal caching, and Table 3 provides useful evidence that combining RALU with caching can further improve latency with moderate metric degradation.
weaknesses: The main empirical case is weaker than the claims suggest. On FLUX, RALU is often only marginally better than simply reducing inference steps, and it is worse than Bottleneck Sampling on GenEval at 4x and essentially tied/slightly worse at 7x. On SD3, RALU improves several quality metrics but still shows nontrivial text-alignment degradation relative to the full model. The paper repeatedly describes degradation as negligible, which is not fully supported.

The ablation evidence is thin for the central design choices. Table 4 only perturbs the NT-DM parameters slightly and reports mixed changes; it does not clearly isolate no NT-DM, no correlated noise, no edge-adaptive stage, random-region upsampling, or all-region early upsampling under matched compute. The upsampling-ratio analysis is qualitative only.

The comparison to baselines raises fairness questions. ToCa performs extremely poorly in some settings and is not matched to the advertised 7x speedup block, while RAS is only used for SD3. The paper does not sufficiently justify whether the baseline hyperparameters are optimal or whether stronger temporal/spatial combinations were considered.

There is a technical inconsistency in the noise-injection derivation. The text says the post-upsampling latent should be brought back to the isotropic rectified-flow trajectory, but Appendix Eq. S2 writes the target covariance with Sigma while Eq. S4 matches to an identity covariance. This may be a typo, but it affects confidence in the mathematical presentation.

Important implementation details for reproducibility are under-specified, including the exact edge-selection ratio used in main experiments, Canny thresholds, patch/mask construction, mapping from decoded image edges to latent patches, numerical search ranges for NT-DM, seeds beyond benchmark image counts, and latency measurement protocol/variance.

The scope is narrow despite broad language. NT-DM is explicitly limited to flow-matching models, experiments are only on two T2I backbones, and there is no evaluation on other samplers, U-Net diffusion models, video, or lower-memory/higher-throughput deployment settings.

Qualitative evidence is extensive but not very diagnostic: many figures are small, zoom-dependent, and selected around artifacts; there is no human preference study or artifact-specific quantitative metric to substantiate the visual-fidelity claims.

Overall, the paper has a plausible and useful idea, but the evidence and technical presentation do not yet justify the strength of the claims for a top-tier acceptance. I would lean weak reject rather than borderline because the core gains are modest/inconsistent and the key ablations/reproducibility details are insufficient.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: inference acceleration for large diffusion transformers. The proposed RALU framework is practically attractive because it is training-free and targets spatial computation, which is complementary to better-studied temporal caching methods.

The method is technically plausible and well motivated. The decomposition of upsampling artifacts into edge-local aliasing and global noise-timestep mismatch is useful, and the three-stage design with edge-selective early upsampling plus NT-DM is a coherent response to these observations.

The empirical results are fairly strong. On FLUX.1-dev and SD3, RALU generally improves image-quality metrics over Bottleneck Sampling and temporal baselines at comparable latency/FLOPs, with reported speedups up to about 7x on FLUX and 3x on SD3. The combination with caching further improves speed with moderate metric degradation.

The evaluation includes multiple automatic metrics for image quality and text alignment, two modern flow-matching DiT backbones, baseline comparisons, qualitative examples, uncurated samples, and appendix details on prompt counts, seeds, stage schedules, and baseline configurations.

The paper is mostly clear and readable. The figures communicate the artifact modes and qualitative differences effectively, and the limitations section correctly notes that NT-DM is currently specialized to flow-matching models.
weaknesses: The evidence for text-alignment superiority is mixed. On FLUX, Bottleneck Sampling has comparable or higher GenEval than RALU at both 4x and 7x speedups, and RALU's T2I-Comp score at 4x is lower than Bottleneck. The paper's language sometimes overstates semantic-alignment gains relative to what the tables show.

The ablation evidence is relatively thin. Table 4 varies the NT-DM parameters but the proposed setting is not uniformly best across metrics, and the upsampling-ratio study is mostly qualitative with only three prompts. There is no full ablation isolating edge selection, early upsampling, correlated noise injection, and timestep distribution matching across the main benchmarks.

Generality is limited. Experiments cover only two text-to-image flow-matching DiTs, both at fixed resolutions/settings. The method's behavior on score-based/DDIM-style diffusion, video DiTs, other resolutions, other upsampling operators, and lower-memory hardware remains untested.

Some implementation details important for reproducibility are underspecified in the main text, such as exact Canny parameters, top-k/upsampling ratios for each setting, numerical-search discretization for NT-DM, and whether code will be released. The appendix helps, but a reproduction would still require filling in several choices.

The evaluation relies entirely on automatic metrics and selected qualitative comparisons. For a perceptual generation method whose main claim is artifact reduction, a human preference study or artifact-specific metric would make the quality claims more convincing.

The speed/latency claims are measured on a single A100 setup, and memory usage is not reported. Since the method mixes resolutions and selected full-resolution tokens, memory and hardware-dependent overheads could matter for practical deployment.

There are minor presentation issues, including some awkward phrasing and a likely typo in Table 4 where GenEval is marked with a downward arrow despite higher being better elsewhere. These do not undermine the contribution but should be cleaned up.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: training-free spatial acceleration for diffusion transformers, a less explored complement to timestep reduction and feature caching.

The proposed RALU design is technically motivated: the paper identifies two concrete failure modes of naive latent upsampling, aliasing near edges and noise/timestep distribution mismatch, and proposes targeted mechanisms for each.

The empirical results are fairly broad for a method paper: experiments include FLUX.1-dev and Stable Diffusion 3, several temporal and spatial baselines, latency/FLOP reporting, quality and alignment metrics, qualitative comparisons, and ablations on edge selection, upsampling ratio, NT-Matching, and upsampler choice.
The method is attractive in practice because it is training-free and appears complementary to temporal acceleration and timestep-distilled models.

The appendix provides useful implementation details, baseline settings, computational metrics, and uncurated qualitative samples, which improves reproducibility compared with many acceleration papers.
weaknesses: The central artifact claims are only partially rigorous. The paper reports artifact ratios and visible examples, but the artifact labeling protocol, annotator details, agreement, and sample sizes are not sufficiently specified; this matters because artifact reduction is a main claimed advantage over Bottleneck Sampling.

The evaluation relies heavily on automatic T2I metrics whose correlation with human preference and artifact perception is imperfect. Given the visual nature of the claimed improvements, a human preference or artifact study would substantially strengthen the evidence.

The claim of negligible quality degradation is overstated in some settings. For example, GenEval drops relative to the full FLUX and SD3 baselines, and the distilled-model combinations in Table 2 show nontrivial declines in ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, and GenEval despite large speedups.

The comparison to baselines may be sensitive to tuning. RALU uses setting-specific schedules, edge ratios, and NT-Matching parameters, while it is not fully clear that each baseline was equally optimized for the same quality-speed tradeoff.

The method is limited to flow-matching DiTs for the full NT-Matching component, and the paper only evaluates two DiT families. Generality to diffusion U-Nets, video DiTs, non-flow schedulers, or other resolutions remains unverified.

Some technical presentation details need tightening. For instance, the appendix derivation appears to contain a covariance inconsistency around the target distribution after upsampling, and the numerical search procedure for JSD minimization is not described enough to be independently reproduced without code.

The approach adds complexity through VAE decoding, edge detection, mixed-resolution token handling, and stage-specific rescheduling; while overhead is reported as small, failure modes for unusual prompts, dense textures, text rendering, or images where edges are not the main artifact-prone regions are not deeply analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant bottleneck for high-resolution diffusion transformers: spatial computation scales poorly, and training-free acceleration is practically useful if reliable.

The proposed decomposition into low-resolution denoising, edge-region early upsampling, and final full-resolution refinement is intuitive and reasonably motivated by the observed aliasing/mismatching failure modes.

The manuscript includes quantitative comparisons on two strong text-to-image DiT backbones, FLUX.1-dev and Stable Diffusion 3, plus ablations for early-upsampling ratio, edge selection, upsampler choice, and NT-Matching.
The method appears complementary to some temporal acceleration and distilled-model settings, which is a useful property if the quality tradeoffs hold in practice.
weaknesses: The main claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims negligible degradation, but Table 1 shows meaningful drops from the base models in several settings, especially SD3 at 3x speedup: ImageReward drops from 0.971 to 0.798, CLIP-IQA from 0.692 to 0.645, and GenEval from 0.703 to 0.599.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on automatic T2I metrics and selected qualitative examples. For a paper whose central claim is artifact removal, the lack of human preference/artifact assessment is a material weakness, especially because metrics such as CLIP-IQA, NIQE, ImageReward, and GenEval may not reliably capture localized aliasing or mismatching artifacts.

The artifact-ratio analysis is under-specified. The manuscript does not clearly define who labels artifacts, how many samples are judged, whether labeling is blinded, or whether inter-rater/statistical uncertainty is measured. This weakens one of the core pieces of evidence for RALU.

The technical derivation/presentation has inconsistencies that raise correctness concerns. For example, the main text describes matching the upsampled latent to an isotropic covariance trajectory, while the appendix states an upsampled conditional distribution with covariance Sigma and then matches to an identity covariance in the following equation. This should be clarified before the method can be confidently assessed.

The baseline comparison may not be fully convincing. Several temporal baselines perform surprisingly poorly under the chosen configurations, and the paper does not demonstrate that baseline hyperparameters were tuned comparably to RALU. Some tables also contain apparent inconsistencies, e.g. Bottleneck SD3 2x latency differs between the main table and supplementary computational table.

Generality is limited. Experiments cover only flow-matching DiT text-to-image models at 1024x1024, while the method's NT-Matching is explicitly tailored to flow-matching architectures. Applicability to other diffusion backbones, other resolutions, image editing, video, or non-flow schedulers is not established.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper reports many hyperparameters, but the algorithm depends on model- and speedup-specific searched values for c, h_k, stage boundaries, and early-upsampling ratio; without code or a clearer optimization recipe, reproducing the exact behavior would be difficult.

The contribution is incremental relative to existing spatial acceleration and multi-resolution sampling ideas. The edge-selective upsampling and timestep/noise matching combination is useful, but the novelty is not strong enough to compensate for the evaluation and clarity issues.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: training-free spatial acceleration for large DiT text-to-image models. The core idea of doing most denoising at low latent resolution while selectively upsampling edge-prone regions is well motivated and useful.

The analysis of two failure modes of naive latent upsampling, aliasing around high-frequency edges and distribution/timestep mismatch after upsampling, gives the method a clear technical basis rather than being only an engineering heuristic.

The proposed RALU framework is simple, modular, and plausibly deployable: it needs no retraining, adds modest overhead for edge detection, and can be combined with temporal acceleration methods and timestep-distilled models.

The experimental evidence is fairly broad for this topic: results are reported on FLUX.1-dev and Stable Diffusion 3, with latency, FLOPs, memory, multiple perceptual/alignment metrics, qualitative comparisons, ablations for upsampling ratio, edge selection, NT-Matching, and integration with other accelerators.

The reported gains are meaningful. For example, RALU gives around 5.5x and 7.0x speedups on FLUX with better ImageReward/CLIP-IQA/NIQE tradeoffs than comparable baselines, and around 2x/3x on SD3 while maintaining competitive alignment metrics.
The supplement strengthens reproducibility by specifying schedules, NT-Matching parameters, baseline settings, hardware, metric protocols, and additional uncurated qualitative samples.
weaknesses: Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. Terms such as artifact-free and negligible quality degradation are overstated: several metrics still degrade relative to the full base models, and combinations with temporal acceleration or distilled models show visible metric drops, especially in CLIP-IQA and GenEval.

The artifact-ratio evaluation is under-specified. The paper reports artifact ratios and uses them centrally to justify the method, but it is not fully clear whether these are manually labeled, automatically detected, how annotators were instructed, or how reliable the labels are.

The method is evaluated only on flow-matching DiTs, and the NT-Matching derivation is tailored to that setting. This is acknowledged, but it limits the generality of the contribution compared with the broader framing of diffusion transformer acceleration.

There are some technical and presentation ambiguities around mixed-resolution processing, including how positional embeddings, attention computation, and token layouts are handled when low- and high-resolution latent tokens coexist. The discussion notes this mechanism is not fully understood, but more implementation detail would be important for reproducibility.

The comparison to baselines is useful but not completely definitive. Baseline configurations appear hand-selected for target speed regimes, and it is unclear whether all competing methods were equally tuned for quality-speed tradeoff. A stronger Pareto comparison over each method's tunable settings would make the evidence more robust.

The quantitative evaluation relies heavily on automatic T2I metrics, which are known to be imperfect proxies for human preference and artifact perception. A small human preference or artifact study would better support the visual-quality claims.

The derivation/notation has minor inconsistencies and rough edges, such as covariance notation differences between the main text and appendix, and the role/constraints of the parameter c could be explained more cleanly. These do not appear fatal but reduce confidence in the technical presentation.
